cite.paraphrase: Here ignorance is the field (kṣetra), the ground of origin, of the later ones — I-am-ness and the rest — which have four varieties: dormant, attenuated, interrupted, fully active. Dormancy (prasupti) is the afflictions' having reached a seed-state (bīja-bhāva), resting in the mind as bare potency (śakti-mātra); their awakening (prabodha) is their coming face to face with a support (ālambana). For one with discerning insight (prasaṃkhyāna) whose seeds of affliction are burnt, even when the support is present the affliction does not arise again; how could a burnt seed sprout? Hence one 'whose afflictions are worn away, skilful, in his last body (carama-deha)' is spoken of; in him alone is that fifth state of the afflictions, the burnt-seed state. Attenuation (tanutva): afflictions struck by the cultivation of their opposite (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) become thin. Interrupted (vicchinna): they act again and again in this or that form, cut off; e.g. at a time of passion anger is not seen, though passion, seen in one place, is not absent in another — Caitra, enamoured of one woman, is not thereby disenchanted with the others; there passion has gained activity, elsewhere it will gain it; so at that time it is dormant, attenuated and interrupted. Fully active (udāra): the one that has gained activity in regard to an object. All these do not go beyond being of the sphere of the afflictions. The bhāṣya notes that these four belong to particular afflictions in particular circumstances: as one is turned back by the cultivation of the opposite, so it becomes manifest through its own manifester's coloration. All the afflictions are varieties of ignorance, because ignorance pervades in all: what ignorance makes appear as a thing, that the afflictions lie along with; they are found at the time of a cognition of error, and are worn away as ignorance is worn away.

Each is again threefold, from greed (lobha, e.g. for meat or skin), from anger ('he wronged me'), or from delusion ('it will be dharma for me'); greed, anger and delusion are each mild, middling or intense. So violence has twenty-seven forms; the mild, middling and intense are again each threefold, making eighty-one; and with rules, options and combinations it is countless, since the kinds of living beings are countless. The same applies to untruth and the rest. 'Suffering and ignorance without end as fruit' is the cultivation of the opposite: the violent one first takes away the victim's strength, then torments him by the fall of a weapon, then deprives him of life. From robbing strength, his own animate and inanimate implements lose strength; from causing suffering he suffers in hells, animal births and ghost-states; and from robbing life, moment by moment at the end of his own life, wishing for death, he still breathes somehow, because the ripening of suffering is fixed. Taṇhā is the origin of suffering (DN 22:19). Jain lobha is a passion-felt deluding karma (kaṣāya-vedanīya, TS 8.9) and a literal cause of karmic matter binding the soul (TS 8.2). (2) Scope: YS rāga covers any remembered pleasure and its means (YB 2.7). Kāmacchanda is sensual desire. Taṇhā in DN 22 also includes craving for being and for non-being (DN 22:19); the Yoga puts the wish to go on being under a different kleśa (abhiniveśa, YS 2.9). Jain lobha comes in four intensities, anantānubandhī to saṃjvalana (TS 8.9), a grading no other lens uses. The Theravāda lists grade it differently, by depth: a hindrance that keeps jhāna from arising (Vism IV), greed as a root of unwholesome consciousness (Vism XIV), and sensual lust as one of the five lower fetters (Vism XXII). (3) What is freed: the Yoga ends in the seer's aloneness (YS 2.25), the suttas in the cessation of craving (DN 22:20), the Jain path in the soul's release from karmic matter (TS 8.2). The self-question behind these three ends is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question in one_truth.json).

Yoga is samādhi, and samādhi is a property of the mind (citta) at every level (sārvabhauma). The levels of the mind (citta-bhūmi) are: scattered (kṣipta), stupefied (mūḍha), distracted (vikṣipta), one-pointed (ekāgra) and stilled (niruddha). In a distracted mind, samādhi that has become subordinate to the distraction does not count on the side of yoga. That samādhi is accompanied by reasoning (vitarka), by reflection (vicāra), by joy (ānanda) or by I-am-ness (asmitā) — Vyāsa says he will set this out later. statement: Asmitā is not pride. YS 2.6 names a confusion of the seer with its instrument, a structural error that is present even without any haughtiness. The Gītā's darpa and abhimāna and the Jain māna are attitudes of self-exaltation: the Gītā lists them among the marks of a bad endowment (BhG 16.4), and TS grades māna in four intensities (TS 8.9). They meet only in the 'I'. Personality view comes closest to asmitā, since both take something that is not the self as the self. The Yoga also counts that as an error (YS 2.5), but it corrects the error by isolating a real seer (YS 2.25). The Visuddhimagga's remedy is to abandon the view, which is one of the five lower fetters, and conceit remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). It does not isolate a seer in the view's place. Whether a seer remains is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question of one_truth.json).

statement: On the sense of 'I': Jain, Yoga, Upaniṣadic and Buddhist texts all teach that one is not the body, nor any passing state of mind. The Yoga Sūtra calls the seer's seeming oneness with the mind 'I-am-ness'; Theravāda texts teach seeing 'this is not mine, I am not this'. cite.paraphrase: Chapter XIV, on the aggregate of formations, continues with the unwholesome. In the first unwholesome consciousness rooted in greed there are seventeen: thirteen given in their own form (contact, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, energy, life faculty, concentration, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, greed, delusion, wrong view) and four "whatever" factors (zeal, resolve, restlessness, attention). cite.paraphrase: The five lower fetters are personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and observances, sensual lust and ill will (paṭigha), which bind to lower aggregates and the like. Defilements (kilesa), being themselves defiled and defiling their associated states, are ten: greed, hate, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Wrongnesses (micchatta) are eight: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration, or ten with wrong release and wrong knowledge. Worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are eight: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain, blame and praise; here the text says liking for what is gained and resentment for what is not gained are taken under those. Avarice (macchariya) is fivefold: over dwelling, family, gain, teaching and praise. Perversions (vipallāsa) are three: of perception, of mind and of view, taking the impermanent, painful, not-self and unlovely as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. Ties (gantha) are four: covetousness, ill will, adherence to rites and observances, and the insistence that "this alone is truth". Wrong courses (agati) are doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done through desire, hate, delusion and fear. Taints (āsava) is a name for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view and ignorance, so called because they flow out (as far as change-of-lineage and the top of existence by way of object, or through the unguarded doors like water through the holes of a jar, in the sense of constant trickling), or because they make the suffering of the round flow (continued on p. 684).

cite.paraphrase: At the moment of the arahat path he emerges from the remaining fetters and latent tendencies (from lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance; the latent conceit, latent lust for existence, latent ignorance), from the defilements that follow them and the aggregates, and outwardly from all signs: as quoted, "understanding in the turning away by emerging in both ways is knowledge in the path". In the development of the eight worldly attainments calm is stronger; in developing the contemplation of impermanence and so on, insight is stronger; in the moment of the noble path they occur yoked together, neither exceeding the other; so in the four knowledges of the paths there is a joining of both powers. The text quotes the Paṭisambhidā: for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration whose domain is cessation; for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by ignorance, insight in the sense of contemplation has cessation as domain; thus in the sense of emerging calm and insight are of one taste, yoked and not exceeding each other. Then, under "what is to be abandoned by which, and the abandoning", the text begins: in these four knowledges one should know what states are to be abandoned by each knowledge, states that come as fetters, defilements, wrongnesses, worldly conditions, avarice, perversions, ties, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, adherences, clingings, latent tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome thoughts. Fetters are ten things that bind beings to aggregates, to the fruit of kamma and to suffering; of them five are higher fetters (lust for fine-material existence, for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) (continued on p. 683).

statement: Asmitā is not pride. YS 2.6 names a confusion of the seer with its instrument, a structural error that is present even without any haughtiness. The Gītā's darpa and abhimāna and the Jain māna are attitudes of self-exaltation: the Gītā lists them among the marks of a bad endowment (BhG 16.4), and TS grades māna in four intensities (TS 8.9). They meet only in the 'I'. Personality view comes closest to asmitā, since both take something that is not the self as the self. The Yoga also counts that as an error (YS 2.5), but it corrects the error by isolating a real seer (YS 2.25). The Visuddhimagga's remedy is to abandon the view, which is one of the five lower fetters, and conceit remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). It does not isolate a seer in the view's place. Whether a seer remains is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question of one_truth.json).

Suttas: restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) is a hindrance known as present or absent (MN 10:36), and a scattered (vikkhitta) mind is known as scattered (MN 10:34). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

cite.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
cite.original: 4. Dhammānupassanā 4.1. Dhammānupassanānīvaraṇapabba Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu nīvaraṇesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ kāmacchandaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ kāmacchando’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa kāmacchandassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa kāmacchandassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ byāpādaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ byāpādo’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa byāpādassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa byāpādassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa byāpādassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ thinamiddhan’ti pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa thinamiddhassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa thinamiddhassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ uddhaccakukkuccan’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa uddhaccakukkuccassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Santaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti, asantaṁ vā ajjhattaṁ vicikicchaṁ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṁ vicikicchā’ti pajānāti; yathā ca anuppannāya vicikicchāya uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannāya vicikicchāya pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnāya vicikicchāya āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.
cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, first section: the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas in dhammas with regard to the five hindrances. Here, when sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is present in him he knows 'there is sensual desire in me'; when it is absent he knows 'there is no sensual desire in me'; he knows how unarisen sensual desire comes to arise; he knows how arisen sensual desire is abandoned; and he knows how the abandoned sensual desire will not arise again in the future. He does the same, in exactly this fivefold way, for ill will (byāpāda), for dullness and drowsiness (thina-middha), for restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) and for doubt (vicikicchā).

statement: Each names a sinking, sorrowful turn of mind. Vyāsa: dejection (daurmanasya) is a disturbance of the mind through the frustration of a wish, and it accompanies distraction (YS 1.31; YB 1.31). Gītā: Arjuna is overcome by pity and despairing (viṣīdan), his mind bewildered about dharma (BhG 1.28, 2.1, 2.7). TS: sorrowful dwelling (ārta-dhyāna) dwells on removing the disagreeable, on keeping the agreeable, on pain, and on longing for future enjoyment (TS 9.30–33). MN 10 declares the four establishments of mindfulness a path to the ending of pain and displeasure (dukkha-domanassa) (MN 10:2). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.
